title: Differentially Private Equilibrium Finding in Polymatrix Games
one_liner: When multiple players find a fair outcome in a game while keeping their moves secret from eavesdroppers, this paper shows the first way to do both at the same time.
lead: Imagine a group of traders who need to find a fair deal, but a hacker is listening. The paper solves a deep puzzle: how many secrets must each trader reveal to find that fair deal? Older algorithms had to pick between keeping secrets and finding a good deal. This paper is the first to achieve both, by using special structure in the game.

paras: Imagine three firms setting prices for widgets. They need to find prices where no firm can raise profit by changing alone, a fair outcome called an equilibrium. But a rival firm is hacking their network to read their messages.

If the firms send unencrypted prices, the eavesdropper learns their strategy instantly. If they encrypt everything, the algorithm cannot find the fair prices—it gets stuck. Every old algorithm trades off one for the other: either the eavesdropper learns nothing but the firms never find a deal, or they find a great deal but the eavesdropper steals their entire playbook.

callout.html: As more players join the game, can we find a fair outcome while the amount of information each player leaks shrinks to nearly zero?

steps.text: Show mathematically that old algorithms cannot fix this: each new player added means more broadcast messages sent, and information leaks grow exponentially with players while fairness gains shrink, creating an impossible bind.
Polymatrix games have a special shape: each player's payoff depends on their own choice plus a few neighbours, not everyone else.
Use this structure: send fewer messages by exploiting who actually talks to whom, not the full graph.
Prove that as player count N rises, the fair-deal quality and the secrecy both improve because fewer messages per player are needed to reach consensus when the game graph is sparse.
Run experiments on actual polymatrix games and confirm the theory holds up in practice.

paras: Every player in a distributed algorithm must send messages to learn everyone's choice. The paper changes which messages get sent: instead of broadcasting to all players, each player sends to only the few neighbours who actually affect their payoff. This cuts the number of messages while keeping the quality of the outcome.

hidden.name: Nash gap
paras: The Nash gap (also called exploitability) is the extra profit a player can grab by changing strategy, if all others stick to the current plan. In a perfect fair outcome (called a Nash equilibrium), this gap is zero: no player gains by moving alone.

The paper tracks two things together: how small the Nash gap gets, and how much secret information the eavesdropper collects (measured in bits of privacy lost per player). It shows both shrink together as more players enter.

heat.caption: Darker means each player can exploit the outcome more. Early players benefit; later players discover the scheme is fair.

reads.html: If players follow the algorithm, the outcome gets closer to fair as the group grows larger.
Nash gap vanishes at rate 1/sqrt(N) while differential privacy budget (epsilon) also shrinks with N, a simultaneous convergence previously impossible.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: exploit the game structure
paras: Polymatrix games have a hidden structure: each player's payoff depends only on their own choice and a small set of neighbours, not all other players. In a supply chain, firm A cares about firm B (its supplier) and firm C (its customer), but not firm M in another industry.

Old algorithms treat all players as equally connected, so they broadcast messages to everyone. This leaks secrets widely. The new algorithm sends messages only along the actual edges in the game graph. Each player communicates only with the neighbours whose choice affects its payoff.

By shrinking the communication network to match the game's actual structure, fewer messages are sent, so less information leaks to the eavesdropper. At the same time, the structural properties guarantee that the algorithm still finds a fair outcome. The two improve together because they are not independent trade-offs—they both stem from reduced communication.

stages.s: Polymatrix game: each player knows their own payoff and their neighbours
Distribute: each player sends to neighbours only, not all players
Update: each player adjusts strategy based on replies from neighbours
Repeat across rounds, averaging to smooth randomness
Strategies converge to a fair outcome with shrinking privacy loss

math.words: As the number of players N grows, the Nash gap shrinks at a rate of 1 divided by the square root of N, while the privacy loss per player also shrinks like 1 divided by the square root of N.
symbols: the most profit any player gains by deviating alone
the eavesdropper's information advantage from listening to one round
number of players in the game
decreases proportional to the square root of player count

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: With N = 4 players: Nash_gap shrinks to roughly 1/sqrt(4) = 1/2 of the baseline unfair payoff.
Privacy loss per player drops to roughly 1/2 of a single-player leak.
With N = 100 players: Nash_gap shrinks to roughly 1/sqrt(100) = 1/10.
Privacy loss drops to 1/10 as well.
Both improve together: more players means fairer deals AND better secrets kept, not a trade-off.

math.note: The square-root rate is the same for both because they share a root cause: smaller communication graphs leak less and still converge.

charts.title: Old algorithms (pick one)
charts.note: Choose secrecy or fairness. Increasing players makes things worse.

charts.title: This paper (both improve)
charts.note: Fairness improves AND privacy loss shrinks simultaneously as players increase because the algorithm sends fewer messages per player when the game graph is sparse, reducing both the unfairness and the eavesdropping window.

items.html: If every player's payoff depends on every other player's choice, the algorithm cannot exploit structure and may revert to old trade-offs.

If the adversary can read all messages (not just a bounded set), the hardness result from the paper applies: reading every message reveals the full strategy, so no matter how the algorithm is designed, information leakage cannot be reduced, and privacy improvement becomes mathematically impossible.
Early rounds have high Nash gap and modest privacy gain. The benefit grows only as N increases or more rounds run, not immediately.
On sparse polymatrix games with local eavesdropping, the algorithm delivers fair outcomes with shrinking information leaks as the group expands.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a three-player economic game where each player sets quantity (quantity competition, like a Cournot market). Player A and B compete directly; Player C buys from both. Run the algorithm with privacy constraints, recording the Nash gap and privacy loss at each round. Plot both metrics: they should both improve as rounds increase or as you add more players because the sparse game structure means fewer messages leak information.
demo.metric_eq: Nash_gap = max_i (payoff_i(deviate) - payoff_i(current)), privacy_loss = bits the eavesdropper learns per player per round
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss: fairness and secrecy rise together, not in opposition.
